In this lesson you will learn about a transistor type known as a MOSFET, or Metal Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor.
INTRODUCTIONM
The MOSFET is a very popular device used in integrated circuit technology because building it is easy and the gate does not draw current like the base of a bipolar transistor.

The MOSFET has many uses in low-power amplifiers and digital circuits, like microprocessors. As MOSFET devices are developed smaller and smaller, their use in many circuits will surpass other more expensive devices, like BJTs...

The gate of the MOSFET is not connected to any other part of the device. So the input resistance to a MOSFET is very high. The operation of the gate is similar to the operation of a capacitor.

Let's look at the operation of the Enhancement-mode NMOS. A voltage is applied to the gate that is large enough to overcome the threshold voltage of the device. For most MOSFETs, this is around 1 volt.lt.around 1 volt.

The voltage applied to the gate in this example is positive with respect to the source. This strong positive voltage causes an attraction of negative charges in the channel between the source and the drain..in...

The threshold voltage is the point where the voltage applied to the gate causes the same number of positive and negative charges in the channel region. Remember, with no voltage the channel is P-type which has an abundance of positive ions...

As we increase the gate voltage above the threshold, a phenomenon called inversion occurs. Inversion occurs when the charge on the gate causes more negative ions in the channel than positive ions. This makes the channel essentially N-type during this condition.
The size of the channel depends on the voltage applied to the gate. Remember the gate draws NO current, only a voltage. This is one advantage of using a MOSFET.

Since the channel is now the same material (N+) as the source and drain, current can flow from the source to the drain. This current is known as the drain current and is dependent on the size of the channel..

It is important to realize that the drain current and the source current are the same. Since there are no other paths for current, current in has to equal current out as stated in Kirchhoff's current law.. current law.

In a sense, a MOSFET is like a water spigot. The gate is the handle, the source is the water supply and the drain is the water outlet. Varying the handle of the spigot allows different amounts of water or current to pass through the spigot........

The structure of the Depletion-mode MOSFET is very similar to the Enhancement-mode version. The difference is that the channel is fabricated of the same doping as the source and drain. This is called a diffused channel. In this example the channel, source and drain are all N-type materials.

With zero or positive voltage applied to the gate, current is free to flow through the channel. s negative voltage is applied, positive ions are drawn into the channel. As the number of positive ions in an area surpasses the negative ions, the material effectively becomes P-type...

As negative voltage from the gate is applied, positive ions are drawn into the channel. As the number of positive ions in the channel surpass the number of negative ions, the material effectively becomes P-type...e.rpasses the negative ions, the material effectively becomes P-type...

The point where the voltage at the gate causes the entire channel to be inverted to P-type is known as pinch-off. In other words, we have pinched off the channel which does not allow current to flow..

We can see that the Depletion-mode MOSFET works opposite of the Enhancement-mode MOSFET. In a Depletion-mode MOSFET when zero volts is applied current flows. In the Enhancement-mode MOSFET when zero volts is applied there is no current flow.

As we increase the voltage applied from the gate, the current decreases in the Depletion-mode MOSFET. As voltage from the gate is increased, current increases in the Enhancement-mode MOSFET.FET..s in the Enhancement-mode MOSFET.

DISCUSSION
MOSFET devices are used for the same applications as transistors in other circuits, like the Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT).
The most common applications are amplifiers and digital logic circuits. Other applications include current mirrors and active loads. We will look at a few common basic circuits utilizing MOSFETs...
Compared here are common source MOSFET and a common emitter BJT amplifier. Look at the graphs for both circuits. They perform similar functions.
Although the curves on the graphs are not identical, the general shapes are the same. Also notice that the circuits are identical except for the transistors themselves.

While the input impedance, output impedance and gain are different for both circuits, the operation is the same. Using your knowledge of a common emitter BJT configuration can predict the operation of the common source MOSFET configuration...
Remember. The common emitter and common source amplifiers are used to provide a relatively high voltage gain.
This MOSFET circuit is of a common gate configuration. Again, notice the common base BJT equivalent circuit has been given. These circuits perform similar functions.

All of the characteristics for the common base configuration can be applied to the common gate configuration. Knowing this information makes analyzing circuits with both BJT and MOSFET stages much easier..
Remember. The common base and common gate amplifiers are used for applications requiring low input impedance, high output impedance, and a current gain of less than one.

The last type of amplifier we are going to look at is the common drain MOSFET amplifier, also known as a Source Follower. Again, the BJT equivalent is shown, the common collector or emitter follower configuration...
These amplifiers are used as an impedance transformer. They have high input impedance, low output impedance and a voltage gain that is close to one. This means no gain, signal in equals signal out...

Just like a BJT, a MOSFET can be used as a switch turned on by the voltage on the gate. Shown below are the switching operations of both an NMOS and PMOS transistor for high and low inputs...
Both the PMOS and NMOS circuits are inverters. Inverters change low voltage levels to high or high voltage levels to low. The resistors in both circuits dissipate power and lower the voltage....
Modern digital circuits use both the NMOS and PMOS transistors in pairs, known as CMOS or complementary MOSFETS. With this type of circuit either the PMOS or the NMOS is on at a particular time...

As the input switches from high to low, VDD or ground is presented at the output. This circuit does not need a resistor to dissipate power or lower voltage. This makes CMOS logic circuits very popular in microprocessors...
